title: Response-surface fit and residuals: how good is the surrogate?
summary: How good is a surrogate model? Compare its predictions with the truth on held-out points. The parity plot shows overall agreement; the residual plots show the structure that R-squared hides.

media.alt: Three panels: left, a parity scatter of surrogate prediction against truth on 0 to 10 with a dashed y = x line, R-squared 0.977 and RMSE 0.47 printed; upper right, residuals against prediction with a dashed zero line, mostly positive at both ends and negative in the middle; lower right, a histogram of residuals centred slightly above zero.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How good is the surrogate?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: truth (x) against surrogate prediction (y), both 0 to 10 and equal scale. Upper right: residual (y) against prediction (x, tick labels hidden). Lower right: residual (x) against count (y).
look_at: Do the points lie on the parity line over the whole range, or do they curve away at the ends?
Are the residuals random around zero, or do they show a pattern against the prediction?
Is the residual histogram centred on zero (no bias)?
Are the points held-out (not used to fit)?
as_drawn: 120 held-out points. R-squared = 0.977 and RMSE = 0.47 are printed in the upper left of the parity panel.
The residual panel is not random: the residuals are positive at low and high predictions and negative in the middle (about -0.3 near 3 to 5), a curved pattern.
The histogram is centred near +0.2, not 0: the surrogate overpredicts by 0.2 on average. That bias accounts for about 18 percent of the mean squared error (0.041 of 0.222).
The x-axis tick labels of the upper right panel are hidden, so the horizontal position (prediction) is not labelled.
read_the_figure.proves: Points near the parity line and unstructured, centred residuals on held-out data show that the surrogate reproduces the truth well over the tested range. Even then the surrogate is trustworthy only inside the range of the held-out data.
if_wrong: A curved pattern in the residuals: the surrogate misses systematic structure that a better model could capture.
A histogram not centred on zero: the surrogate is biased.
Residuals growing with the prediction: the error is multiplicative, and a log scale or a weighting is needed.
must_check: parity line: it is the reference for perfect agreement, so deviations can be seen as distances from it.
residual panel: R-squared and RMSE are summaries that hide structure; the residual plot is the diagnostic.

terms.meaning: A fast approximate model of an expensive function or simulation.
Points not used to fit the surrogate, which give an honest estimate of its error.
Prediction against truth; points on y = x mean perfect agreement.
Prediction minus truth for one point.
The fraction of the truth's variance explained by the surrogate.
The mean residual; a systematic over- or underprediction.

remember: MSE = bias^2 + variance of the residuals.
R^2 = 1 - RMSE^2 / sigma_y^2: a wide range of the truth inflates R^2.
Residuals against prediction should look like noise with no pattern.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: each dot is one held-out point, truth on x and prediction on y, with the dashed amber line y = x. Right: the same points as residuals, against the prediction in the upper panel and as a histogram in the lower panel. Colour distinguishes the panels; the dashed amber line marks zero in both.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: a good surrogate gives the same number as the true model. On the parity plot that means points on the diagonal. But a good-looking diagonal can hide a lot, because the eye cannot see a gap of 0.3 on a scale of 10. Plotting the residuals magnifies the gaps and shows whether they are random noise or a pattern, which would mean the surrogate has a systematic fault.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: R-squared of 0.977 sounds nearly perfect but depends on how widely the truth varies; the same surrogate on a narrower range would score lower. The parity plot compresses the error to the diagonal. A histogram centred near zero can hide a pattern that cancels (positive at the ends and negative in the middle). And held-out points inside the training range say nothing about extrapolation.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot residuals against each input variable to find which one drives the pattern. A cross-validated error with an interval is a more honest number than one split. For a surrogate used inside an optimisation, check the error near the optimum, not only on average.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a smoothed line (a running mean) through the residuals to expose the pattern, label the x axis of the residual panel, print the bias and the fraction of MSE due to bias, and add the training points in a different colour.

worked.title: Reading the surrogate check of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What do R-squared and RMSE say, and are they consistent? (2) What does the residual panel show that the summary numbers do not? (3) How much of the error is bias?

solution.text: (1) R-squared 0.977 and RMSE 0.47. For truth spread uniformly over 0 to 10 (variance 8.33) the implied R-squared is 1 - 0.47^2 / 8.33 = 0.973, consistent with 0.977.
(2) A pattern: the residuals are positive below a prediction of about 1.5 and above 6, negative between 2 and 5, so the surrogate has a systematic wave-like error that a single number cannot reveal.
(3) The histogram is centred near +0.2. The bias squared is a share of the mean squared error.

worked.answer: R-squared 0.977 and RMSE 0.47 are consistent; the residuals show a systematic pattern, and a bias of 0.2 makes up about 18 percent of the squared error.

analyze.q: R-squared is 0.977, yet the residuals show a pattern. What would you do next?
analyze.hint: Improve the surrogate where the pattern is.

analyze.q: Why would the same surrogate have a lower R-squared on a narrower input range?
analyze.hint: R-squared compares the error with the spread of the truth.

analyze.q: The histogram is centred at 0.2. Does that matter if the surrogate is used inside an optimiser?
analyze.hint: A constant bias does not move a minimum; a pattern does.

evaluate.q: Would you use this surrogate to replace the expensive model in a design study?
evaluate.hint: Range, pattern, error near the region of interest.

create: Add a running mean through the residual panel and label its x axis.
Compute and print the share of the squared error due to bias on the figure.

checks.q: Why look at residuals as well as R-squared?
checks.hint: What can a single number hide?
checks.answer: R-squared is one summary and can be high while the errors are systematic; the residual plot shows structure and bias.

checks.q: RMSE 0.5 and truth variance 10. What is R-squared?
The residuals are positive at both ends and negative in the middle. What does this tell you about the surrogate's form?
checks.answer: It misses a curvature (a quadratic-like term) in the truth; adding a quadratic term or using a more flexible surrogate would remove the pattern.
